paragraphs: “How do you know? How can you speak so confidently?” Alyosha asked sharply, frowning.
“Why do you ask, and why are you frightened by my answer? It shows you know I’m telling the truth.”
“You don’t like Ivan. Ivan wouldn’t be tempted by money.”
“Really? And Katerina Ivanovna’s beauty? It isn’t only the money, though a fortune of sixty thousand is an attraction.”
“Ivan is above that. He wouldn’t chase after anyone for thousands. It’s not money, not comfort, that Ivan is seeking. Perhaps it’s suffering he’s seeking.”
“What wild dream is this now? Oh, you—aristocrats!”
“Ah, Misha, he has a stormy spirit. His mind is in bondage. He is haunted by a great, unsolved doubt. He is one of those who don’t want millions, but an answer to their questions.”

“That’s plagiarism, Alyosha. You’re quoting your elder’s phrases. Ah, Ivan has set you a problem!” cried Rakitin, with open malice. His face changed, and his lips twitched. “And it’s a stupid problem. There’s no use guessing at it. Rack your brains—you’ll understand it. His article is absurd and ridiculous. And did you hear his stupid theory just now: if there’s no immortality of the soul, then there’s no virtue, and everything is lawful. (And by the way, do you remember how your brother Mitya cried out: ‘I will remember!’) An attractive theory for scoundrels!—(I’m being abusive, that’s stupid.) Not for scoundrels, but for pedantic _poseurs_, ‘haunted by profound, unsolved doubts.’ He’s showing off, and what it all comes down to is ‘on the one hand we cannot but admit’ and ‘on the other it must be confessed!’ His whole theory is a fraud! Humanity will find in itself the power to live for virtue even without believing in immortality. It will find it in love for freedom, for equality, for fraternity.”
Rakitin could hardly hold himself back in his heat, but suddenly, as though remembering something, he stopped short.
“Well, that’s enough,” he said, with a still more twisted smile. “Why are you laughing? Do you think I’m a vulgar fool?”

“No, I never dreamed of thinking you a vulgar fool. You’re clever but ... never mind, it was silly of me to smile. I understand your getting hot about it, Misha. I guess from your warmth that you aren’t indifferent to Katerina Ivanovna yourself; I’ve suspected that for a long time, brother, and that’s why you don’t like my brother Ivan. Are you jealous of him?”
“And jealous of her money, too? Aren’t you going to add that?”
“I won’t say anything about money. I’m not going to insult you.”

“I believe you, since you say so, but confound you, and your brother Ivan with you. Don’t you understand that a person might very well dislike him, quite apart from Katerina Ivanovna? And why the devil should I like him? He condescends to abuse me, you know. Why haven’t I the right to abuse him?”
“I never heard him say anything about you, good or bad. He doesn’t speak of you at all.”

“But I heard that the day before yesterday at Katerina Ivanovna’s he was abusing me for all he was worth—you see what an interest he takes in your humble servant. And which of us is the jealous one after that, brother, I can’t say. He was good enough to give the opinion that if I don’t go in for the career of an archimandrite in the near future and become a monk, I’ll be sure to go to Petersburg and get a place on some solid magazine as a reviewer, that I’ll write for it for ten years, and in the end become the owner of the magazine and bring it out on the liberal and atheistic side, with a socialistic tinge, with a tiny gloss of socialism, but keeping a sharp lookout all the time, that is, keeping in with both sides and hoodwinking the fools. According to your brother, the tinge of socialism won’t stop me from putting the profits aside and investing them under the guidance of some Jew, until at the end of my career I build a great house in Petersburg and move my publishing offices into it, and let out the upper floors to lodgers. He has even chosen the place for it, near the new stone bridge across the Neva, which they say is to be built in Petersburg.”
“Ah, Misha, that’s just what will really happen, every word of it,” cried Alyosha, unable to hold back a good-humored smile.
“You’re pleased to be sarcastic, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch.”

“No, no, I’m joking, forgive me. I have something quite different on my mind. But excuse me, who can have told you all this? You can’t have been at Katerina Ivanovna’s yourself when he was talking about you?”

“I wasn’t there, but Dmitri Fyodorovitch was, and I heard him tell it with my own ears. If you want to know, he didn’t tell me; I overheard him, unintentionally, of course, because I was sitting in Grushenka’s bedroom and couldn’t leave, since Dmitri Fyodorovitch was in the next room.”
“Oh, yes, I’d forgotten she was a relation of yours.”
“A relation! That Grushenka a relation of mine!” cried Rakitin, turning crimson. “Are you mad? You’re out of your mind!”
“Why, isn’t she a relation of yours? I heard so.”

“Where can you have heard it? You Karamazovs brag of being an ancient, noble family, though your father used to run about playing the buffoon at other men’s tables and was only let into the kitchen as a favor. I may be only a priest’s son, and dirt in the eyes of noblemen like you, but don’t insult me so lightly and recklessly. I have a sense of honor, too, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I couldn’t be a relation of Grushenka, a common harlot. I insist that you understand that!”
Rakitin was extremely irritated.

“Forgive me, for goodness’ sake, I had no idea ... besides ... how can you call her a harlot? Is she ... that sort of woman?” Alyosha flushed suddenly. “I tell you again, I heard she was a relation of yours. You often go to see her, and you told me yourself you’re not her lover. I never dreamed that you of all people had such contempt for her! Does she really deserve it?”

“I may have reasons of my own for visiting her. That’s not your business. But as for relationship, your brother, or even your father, is more likely to make her your relation than mine. Well, here we are. You’d better go to the kitchen. Hello! What’s wrong, what is it? Are we late? They can’t have finished dinner so soon! Have the Karamazovs been making trouble again? No doubt they have. Here’s your father, and your brother Ivan after him. They’ve broken out from the Father Superior’s. And look, Father Isidor’s shouting something after them from the steps. And your father’s shouting and waving his arms. I expect he’s swearing. Bah, and there goes Miüsov driving off in his carriage. You see, he’s leaving. And there’s old Maximov running!—there must have been a row. There can’t have been any dinner. Surely they haven’t been beating the Father Superior! Or have they, perhaps, been beaten? It would serve them right!”
There was good reason for Rakitin’s outcries. A scandalous, unprecedented scene had taken place. It had all come out of the impulse of a moment.
